##########################
### Research Questions ###
##########################

RQ1: What are current sentiments from those who are deaf/Deaf/Hard-of-hearing about assistive technology?

RQ2: How effective have current assistive technologies been at overcoming recurring communication barriers?



################
### Codebook ###
################


Assistive Technology Frame: What technological tools exist to support d/Deaf/Hard-of-hearing people and what do they do

Deaf Sentiment Frame: How do d/Deaf/Hard-of-hearing perceive, interact, and feel about assistive technology

Communication Barriers Frame: The problems that cause communication dysfunction between d/Deaf/Hard-of-hearing people and hearing people


Category: Assistive Technology

1) Sign Language Technology: Any technological tool that recognizes, produces, translates, transmits, teaches, documents, or otherwise mediates a signed language. The sign language itself is core to the function, services such as closed-captioning do not count.


Category: Deaf Sentiment

1) Deaf: "Capital D" Deaf refers to individuals with limited or no hearing capacity who identify as part of the Deaf community and engage with Deaf culture, history, and signed language. 

2) deaf: "Lowercase d" deaf refers to individuals with limited or no hearing capacity without the implication of a connection to Deaf culture.  People who are deaf may or may not use signed languages and might not identify with the broader Deaf community. This term is often used when focusing on the physical aspect of hearing capacity rather than the cultural aspect.

3) Hard-of-hearing: A partial loss of hearing generally ranked from mildly to moderately diminished hearing capacity, but not total loss. Total loss is known as d/Deaf.


Category: Communication Barriers

1) Recurring Communication Barrier: A spectrum of any obstacle that prevents or limits quality and efficiency of communication in terms of tone, information, and purpose between d/Deaf/hard-of-hearing people and others.

2) Language Deprivation: Limited or absent access to a fully accessible first language during critical developmental periods, resulting in lasting gaps in language acquisition, literacy, or communication access.

How can this code be adapted to reformat docx files to .txt files instead of RTF files? Give me the line by line changes without much fluff please, just straight to the point. "

# This was the response that claude gave:

Changes, in order:

1. Load a package that reads docx (your “Load required packages” comment has no code under it):

r
library(officer)   # or: library(readtext)

2. File pattern:

r
# Before
rtf_files <- list.files(path = input_folder, pattern = "\\.RTF$", full.names = TRUE)

# After
docx_files <- list.files(path = input_folder, pattern = "\\.docx$", full.names = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE)

ignore.case = TRUE handles .DOCX too. Also, ~$ temp files that Word creates can match the pattern; filter them out:

r
docx_files <- docx_files[!grepl("^~\\$", basename(docx_files))]

3. Loop variable:

r
# Before
for (file in rtf_files) {
# After
for (file in docx_files) {

4. Read function (replace read_rtf(file)):

With officer:

r
doc <- read_docx(file)
docx_content <- docx_summary(doc)$text

Or with readtext (simpler):

r
docx_content <- readtext::readtext(file)$text

5. Update the variable name in writeLines (to match whichever you used above):

r
writeLines(docx_content, output_file)

Everything else (file_name, output_file, the cat() lines) stays the same. Optionally update the progress message wording.

Full adapted version (officer):

r
library(officer)

input_folder <- "./Deaf-Technology-Sentiment-NexisUni-Database/Articles/"
output_folder <- "./DTS_articles_raw_text/"

if (!dir.exists(output_folder)) dir.create(output_folder)

docx_files <- list.files(path = input_folder, pattern = "\\.docx$", full.names = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE)
docx_files <- docx_files[!grepl("^~\\$", basename(docx_files))]

for (file in docx_files) {
  file_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(file))
  
  doc <- read_docx(file)
  docx_content <- docx_summary(doc)$text
  
  output_file <- file.path(output_folder, paste0(file_name, ".txt"))
  writeLines(docx_content, output_file)
  
  cat("Converted:", file, "to", output_file, "\n")
}

cat("Conversion complete!\n")

Note: docx_summary() also returns table cell text and can include NA for empty paragraphs. If you see blank/NA lines, add docx_content <- docx_content[!is.na(docx_content)] before writing.

# Raw text compiler

```{r include=FALSE}
#This creates an index with the file path to the stories. And then it compiles the stories into a dataframe
#####################
# Begin SM Code #####
#####################

###
# List out text files that match pattern .txt, create DF
###

#Adjust this line for your file name
files <- list.files("./DTS_articles_raw_text", pattern="*.txt") %>% 
  as.data.frame() |> 
  rename(filename = 1) |> 
  #create an matching file name
  mutate(index = str_replace_all(filename, ".txt", "")) %>%
  mutate(index = tolower(gsub("[[:punct:][:space:]|]", "", index))) |> 
  mutate(index = tolower(index)) |> 
  mutate(index = str_sub(index, 1, 25)) |> 
  distinct(index, .keep_all = TRUE)


#Join the file list to the index

final_data <- DTS |> 
  clean_names() |> 
   #create an matching file name
  mutate(index = tolower(gsub("[[:punct:][:space:]|]", "", title))) |> 
  mutate(index = tolower(index)) |> 
  mutate(index = str_sub(index, 1, 25)) |> 
  distinct(index, .keep_all = TRUE)
```

# I was confused why a file was lost in final_index, so I consulted Claude. This was my prompt


final_index <- final_data |> 
  inner_join(files, c("index")) |> 
#you need the actual hard-coded path on this line below to the text
  mutate(filepath = paste0("./DTS_articles_raw_text/", filename))

head(final_index)
Why did this remove a row?


# This was it's response: 
Because inner_join() only keeps rows that have a match in both tables. Any row in final_data whose index value doesn’t appear in files gets dropped (and vice versa).

Common causes of a non-match:

Missing file. A row in final_data has no corresponding file in files (e.g., a docx that failed to convert, or was skipped by the ~$ filter).
Type mismatch. index is numeric in one table and character in the other.
Formatting differences. Whitespace, leading zeros, or case ("001" vs "1", "abc " vs "abc").
NA values. NA in index can fail to match in some cases.

Find the culprit with anti_join():

r
# Rows in final_data with no match in files
final_data |> anti_join(files, by = "index")

# Rows in files with no match in final_data
files |> anti_join(final_data, by = "index")

Check types and duplicates:

r
class(final_data$index); class(files$index)

sum(duplicated(files$index))
sum(duplicated(final_data$index))

Fixes:

If you want to keep all rows from final_data regardless of match, switch to left_join():
r
  final_data |> 
    left_join(files, by = "index") |> 
    mutate(filepath = paste0("./DTS_articles_raw_text/", filename))

Unmatched rows will have NA for filename and filepath.

If it’s a type mismatch, coerce first:
r
  files <- files |> mutate(index = as.character(index))
  final_data <- final_data |> mutate(index = as.character(index))
If it’s whitespace, use trimws() on both index columns.

If you paste the output of the anti_join() and the class() checks, I can tell you which one it is.

```{r}
# Rows in final_data with no match in files
final_data |> anti_join(files, by = "index")

# Rows in files with no match in final_data
files |> anti_join(final_data, by = "index")
```

#Text compiler
# I ran into a problem here as one of the rows in final_index has an NA value in filename, this was caused by one of the files being named weirdly and R not liking how it's imported. I consulted claude and the next code block targets the specific file to let it through, the code block after is the actual compiler

```{r}
final_index <- final_index |> 
  mutate(
    filename = if_else(
      is.na(filename) & grepl("digitally", title, ignore.case = TRUE),
      "&#8216;We arent fully digitally included.txt",
      filename
    ),
    filepath = paste0("./DTS_articles_raw_text/", filename)
  )
```

```{r}
###
# Define function to loop through each text file 
###

create_article_text <- function(row_value) {
  
  #row_value is the single argument that is passed to the function
  # Take each row of the dataframe
  temp <- final_index %>%
    slice(row_value)
  
  # Store the filename for  use in constructing articles dataframe
  temp_filename <- temp$filename
  
  # Create a dataframe by reading in lines of a given textfile
  # Add a filename column 
  articles_df_temp <- read_lines(temp$filepath) %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    mutate(filename = temp_filename)
  
  # Bind results to master articles_df
  # <<- returns to global environment
  articles_df <<- articles_df %>%
    bind_rows(articles_df_temp)
}

###
# Create elements needed to run function
###

# Create empty tibble to store results
articles_df <- tibble()
#running once to test
#create_article_text(2) 
# Create an array of numbers to loop through, from 1 to the number of rows in our index dataframe 
row_values <- 1:nrow(final_index)

###
# Execute function using lapply
# This loops through each row of the dataframe and append results to master file
###

lapply(row_values, create_article_text)

###
# Clean up articles_df and join to index dataframe
###

articles_df <- articles_df %>%
  select(filename, sentence=value) %>%
  inner_join(final_index)


write_csv(articles_df, "DTS_articles_fulltext.csv")

```

# Asked claude to help with the regex for detecting the right strings based on the codebook
```{r}
coded_df <- articles_df |>
  mutate(
    assistive_tech = case_when(
      str_detect(sentence, regex("sign[- ]language|\\bASL\\b|\\bBSL\\b|signed language", ignore_case = TRUE)) &
        str_detect(sentence, regex("app\\b|avatar|glove|translat|recogni|software|\\bAI\\b|artificial intelligence|video relay|\\bVRS\\b|wearable|algorithm", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Sign Language Technology",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),

    deaf_sentiment = case_when(
      str_detect(sentence, "\\bDeaf\\b") ~ "Deaf",
      str_detect(sentence, "\\bdeaf\\b") ~ "deaf",
      str_detect(sentence, regex("hard[- ]of[- ]hearing|hearing loss|\\bHoH\\b", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Hard-of-hearing",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),

    comm_barriers = case_when(
      str_detect(sentence, regex("language deprivation|language delay|delayed language|language acquisition|language access", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Language Deprivation",
      str_detect(sentence, regex("barrier|miscommunicat|inaccessib|exclusion|isolat|lack of access|unable to communicate", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Recurring Communication Barrier",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )
```

# Combining articles back into DTS with their coded matches, TRUE or FALSE depending on if they matched with a category. Claude also assisted with this part. 
```{r}
article_with_code <- coded_df |>
  group_by(filename) |>
  summarise(
    flag_assistive_tech = any(!is.na(assistive_tech)),
    flag_deaf_sentiment = any(!is.na(deaf_sentiment)),
    flag_comm_barriers  = any(!is.na(comm_barriers)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(flag_any = if_any(starts_with("flag_"), ~ .x))
```

```{r}
DTS_with_code <- final_index |>
  left_join(article_with_code, by = "filename") |>
  select(any_of(names(DTS)), starts_with("flag_"))
```

# DTS_with_code is now our original DTS_articles.csv but now with each article marked for if they fall into a given category of the codebook.

# The overall process of all the above code can be described as: Take in DTS_articles as DTS -> convert each row in DTS's corresponding docx to txt -> Compile txt files -> Search through each sentence of each article from the compiled output for code matches from codebook -> Take yes or no results from matching and condense it down to each article is now marked yes or no for if it fell into a given category -> Now we have DTS_with_code, the original DTS_articles.csv but with 3 extra columns that correspond to if the given article had content that matched under a given category
